summary:
Glacier Guardian Kyrgyzstan is an interactive web app for investigating how the climate around Kyrgyzstan’s glaciers is changing, and whether those changes are statistically real.

Its core is a Trend Detective. A user picks a region (7 glacier areas of the Tien Shan and Pamir-Alay), a variable (air temperature, precipitation, snow water, snow cover, glacier runoff or albedo) and a season. The app then builds a 1980–2025 time series from NASA MERRA-2 data and tests it with Sen’s slope, the Mann–Kendall test and linear regression with a t-test and 95% confidence interval. It explains the result in plain language and compares all regions side by side. This shows that the same climate can push neighbouring valleys in opposite directions.

Around this core, a 3D map shows all 7,447 glaciers (RGI 6.0, GLIMS) over NASA GIBS imagery, along with each glacier’s ice loss and PyGEM-OGGM projections to 2100. Users can create an account and submit their own geotagged glacier photos.

This matters because Kyrgyzstan’s glaciers feed the rivers of Central Asia, yet trends are often reported without checking whether they are significant. Our tool lets students, residents and decision-makers verify that themselves.
details:
What it does and how it works

Trend Detective (the core). The user answers three questions: Where?, What? and When?

The app takes monthly NASA MERRA-2 data (1980–2025) for the chosen region and averages it into one value per year for the chosen season. Winter (DJF) uses December of the previous year.

It then runs three tests:

Sen’s slope is the headline rate of change per decade. It is robust to single unusual years.

The Mann–Kendall test decides significance at p < 0.05. It needs no assumption of a straight line or a normal distribution.

Linear regression with a t-test and 95% confidence interval is shown for comparison.

The verdict is written in plain language, and the limitations, such as autocorrelation, are stated.

Every series can be viewed as a table or downloaded as CSV. A region comparison runs the same test across all 7 regions.

Two guided demos walk users through real findings:

spring warming that is significant in every region;

winter snow cover rising in the inner Tien Shan while falling in the Alay.

Glacier map. A 3D MapLibre map shows 7,447 glaciers from RGI 6.0 with names from GLIMS, over NASA GIBS satellite imagery and terrain.

Clicking a glacier shows its area, elevation, mass-balance rate and PyGEM-OGGM projections under three emission scenarios.

It also links to “Trends in this area”, which opens the Trend Detective for the nearest region.

Citizen science. Users sign up, sign in, and send geotagged glacier photos to their personal account.

Each photo is matched to the nearest glacier and can be compared with NASA imagery of the same spot.

Data, all from NASA Earthdata

Source Collections Used for

MERRA-2 M2TMNXSLV, M2TMNXFLX, M2TMNXLND, M2TMNXGLC climate time series for the Trend Detective

RGI 6.0 (NSIDC-0770) and GLIMS (NSIDC-0272) — glacier outlines and names

PyGEM-OGGM (NSIDC) — glacier mass change and projections

NASA GIBS — map imagery

We checked our processed values against the original NASA files.

Benefits and intended impact

Shows what is real. Anyone can tell a real trend from year-to-year noise without statistics training.

Local and comparable. It shows local differences that national averages hide.

Usable in classrooms. Teachers and students get ready demos and downloadable data.

Field observations over time. Hikers and residents can record glacier changes in the field, and those observations build up over time.

Tools and technologies

Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using MapLibre GL for the map and the NASA GIBS WMTS service for imagery. Statistics are written from scratch in JavaScript and checked by unit tests against textbook values.

Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, netCDF4 and pyshp. Data comes through NASA CMR search, OPeNDAP subsetting and Earthdata Login.

Back end: a Python standard-library server with SQLite.

Passwords are stored as PBKDF2 hashes, and sessions use HttpOnly cookies.

Each user can see only their own photos.

Languages: the interface is available in Russian and English.

Creativity

A detective story. Instead of a static dashboard, the user answers where, what and when, then gets a verdict with evidence.

Two methods side by side. The robust and the classical method are shown together. When they disagree, the app explains why: one unusual winter (Naryn, 2022) inflates the regression slope.

Space and ground in one place. The satellite archive and on-the-ground photos sit side by side.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: sources and p-values are stated, and limitations are explained.

Data rule: we used only NASA Earthdata sources, as the challenge requires.

Accessibility: plain-language definitions, a table view for every chart, and a phone layout.

Privacy: user data is never public, and passwords are never stored in plain text.

Low cost: no paid services and no heavy dependencies.
